Computer Vision for the Humanities: Deep Learning for Image Classification¶

Source lesson (two parts): Part 1 and Part 2 of "Computer Vision for the Humanities: An Introduction to Deep Learning for Image Classification," by Daniel van Strien, Kaspar Beelen, Melvin Wevers, Thomas Smits, and Katherine McDonough, Programming Historian 11 (2022). CC-BY 4.0.

This is my second tutorial on the computer vision technique, alongside my facial-recognition notebook. Where that lesson used a pre-trained, off-the-shelf model (Haar Cascade + DeepFace) with no training step of my own, this lesson goes a level deeper: it walks through actually training a deep learning image classifier from scratch (via transfer learning) using the fastai library.

Run this in Google Colab with a GPU runtime. Unlike my facial-recognition notebook, this one needs a GPU to train in a reasonable time: Runtime → Change runtime type → T4 GPU before running anything.

Dataset: Both parts use visual content extracted from the Library of Congress's Chronicling America digitized newspapers, via the Newspaper Navigator project:

  • Part 1 classifies ~1880s newspaper advertisements as "illustrated" vs. "text-only."
  • Part 2 classifies newspaper photos (1895-1920) by what's depicted (human, animal, map, etc.) — a multi-label problem, since one photo can show more than one thing.

Both datasets are hosted on Zenodo (a permanent, DOI-backed archive — I checked, and unlike my first notebook's dead Google Drive link, these download links are still live):

  • Ads data: ads_upsampled.csv + images.zip (~48MB)
  • Photos data: multi_label.csv + images.zip (~880MB — this one's a big download, be patient)

Learning Outcomes¶

By the end of this notebook I should be able to:

  • Explain supervised learning and how it differs from hand-written rules
  • Explain what transfer learning is and why it helps even on historical images very different from a model's original training data
  • Train an image classifier in fastai, for both single-label and multi-label classification
  • Choose an appropriate evaluation metric for imbalanced data, and read a precision/recall/F1 report
  • Explain why classification schemes inevitably simplify visual/historical content

Prior Skills Assumed¶

  • Basic Python 3 and pandas familiarity
  • Comfort with Jupyter/Colab notebooks
  • No prior deep learning background needed (the lesson explains it from scratch)

A Quick Introduction to Machine Learning¶

The lesson introduces supervised learning by contrasting it with hand-written rules. Imagine building a spam filter:

count number spam_words in email:
    if number spam_words >= 10:
        email = spam

This works, until spammers adapt and the rule stops matching reality. Supervised learning flips the approach: instead of writing the rule by hand, you give the computer many labeled examples (spam / not spam) and let it find the pattern itself. The tradeoff: you need labeled training data, and the resulting model's internal "rule" is much harder for a human to read and explain than the hand-written version.

Reflection question 1: In your own words, what's the core tradeoff between a hand-written rule system and a supervised learning model? Think about what each approach needs upfront versus what each gives up.

Part 1: Classifying Newspaper Advertisements¶

Loading the Data¶

fastai's ImageDataLoaders.from_csv reads a CSV of filenames + labels and wires up the corresponding image files automatically. Key arguments:

  • fn_col / label_col: which CSV columns hold the filename and the label
  • item_tfms=Resize(224, ResizeMethod.Squish): every image gets squished to a uniform 224×224 pixels (the model needs a fixed input size)
  • seed=42: fixes the random train/validation split so results are reproducible run to run
In [18]:
from fastai.vision.all import *

%matplotlib inline
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.style.use('seaborn-v0_8')

ad_data = ImageDataLoaders.from_csv(
    path="ads_data/",  # root path to csv file and image directory
    csv_fname="ads_upsampled.csv",  # the name of our csv file
    folder="images/",  # the folder where our images are stored
    fn_col="file",  # the file column in our csv
    label_col="label",  # the label column in our csv
    item_tfms=Resize(224, ResizeMethod.Squish),  # resize images by squishing so they are 224x224 pixels
    seed=42,  # set a fixed seed to make results more reproducible
)

ad_data.show_batch()

Creating and Training the Model¶

Rather than building a neural network from scratch, I'm using transfer learning: starting from resnet18, a model already trained on ImageNet (1.3 million everyday photos), then fine-tuning it on my much smaller newspaper-ad dataset. The early layers of a CNN tend to learn very general features (edges, textures, shapes) that transfer well to almost any image task, even one as different from ImageNet as a 19th-century newspaper scan — I only need to retrain the later, more task-specific layers.

learn.fine_tune(5) runs 5 training epochs (full passes over the training data).

In [19]:
learn = vision_learner(
    ad_data,  # the data the model will be trained on
    resnet18,  # the type of model we want to use
    metrics=accuracy,  # the metrics to track
)

learn.fine_tune(5)

Part 2: Multi-Label Classification of Newspaper Photos¶

Part 1 was single-label: every ad was either "illustrated" or "text-only," never both. Newspaper photos are messier — a single photo might show a person and a building and a vehicle. That calls for multi-label classification, where each image can get zero, one, or several labels at once, rather than being forced into exactly one bucket.

Looking at the Data¶

The labels in multi_label.csv come from Newspaper Navigator's own machine-learning predictions (not human annotation), so they contain errors — "good enough" depends on what you're using them for. Multiple labels on one row are separated by |.

Loading Multi-Label Data, with Augmentation¶

A few new arguments compared to Part 1's ImageDataLoaders.from_csv:

  • label_delim="|": tells fastai that a single label-column value can contain multiple labels, split on |
  • valid_pct=0.3: 30% of the data held out for validation (checking whether the model generalizes, not just memorizes)
  • batch_tfms: image augmentations (random rotation, zoom, flip) applied on the GPU per-batch — these create synthetic variation in the training data for free, without needing any new labeled images, which helps the model generalize better on a dataset this size.
In [29]:
photo_data = ImageDataLoaders.from_df(
    df,  # the dataframe where our labels and image file paths are stored
    folder="photo_data/images",  # the path to the directory holding the images
    bs=32,  # the batch size (number of images + labels per step)
    label_delim="|",  # the deliminator between each label in our label column
    item_tfms=Resize(224),  # resize each image to 224x224
    valid_pct=0.3,  # use 30% of the data as validation data
    seed=42,  # set a seed to make results more reproducible
)

tfms = setup_aug_tfms([Rotate(max_deg=90, p=0.75), Zoom(), Flip()])

photo_data = ImageDataLoaders.from_df(
    df,
    folder="photo_data/images",
    bs=32,
    label_delim="|",
    item_tfms=Resize(224),
    batch_tfms=[*tfms],  # pass in our augmentations
    valid_pct=0.3,
    seed=42,
)

photo_data.show_batch(unique=True, figsize=(10, 10))

Creating and Training the Model¶

This time I'm switching from resnet18 to densenet121 — partly to show how easily fastai lets you swap architectures (one argument), and partly because DenseNet-style models tend to do well on this kind of multi-label task. The metrics also change: F1ScoreMulti() and accuracy_multi are the multi-label versions of the single-label metrics from Part 1, since a plain accuracy score doesn't make sense once an image can have several correct labels at once.

learn.lr_find() runs a quick search to suggest a good learning rate before committing to a full training run.

In [30]:
learn = vision_learner(photo_data, densenet121, metrics=[F1ScoreMulti(), accuracy_multi])

learn.lr_find()
Out[30]:
SuggestedLRs(valley=0.002511886414140463)

learn.fit_one_cycle(5, lr_max=2e-2)
learn.recorder.plot_loss()

Unfreezing for Fine-Tuning¶

So far, only the model's final (task-specific) layers have been training — the pretrained ImageNet layers underneath were "frozen." learn.unfreeze() allows the whole network to keep training, using a slice() of learning rates so earlier (more general) layers change slowly while later (more task-specific) layers change faster. SaveModelCallback automatically keeps the best-performing version by F1 score, in case a later epoch overfits and gets worse.

In [32]:
learn.save('stage_1')

learn.unfreeze()
learn.lr_find()
Out[32]:
SuggestedLRs(valley=0.0003981071640737355)
In [33]:
learn.fit_one_cycle(4, lr_max=slice(6e-6, 4e-4), cbs=[SaveModelCallback(monitor='f1_score')])
epoch train_loss valid_loss f1_score accuracy_multi time

1 0.239792 0.216657 0.555008 0.919583 01:22
2 0.240789 0.212855 0.559469 0.922083 01:20
3 0.234247 0.216172 0.554399 0.919583 01:20

Evaluating the Model¶

learn.get_preds() returns each validation image's predicted probability for every label (not a hard yes/no), so I pick a probability threshold (0.50) above which a label counts as "predicted." classification_report from scikit-learn then breaks down precision, recall, and F1 per label, rather than one blended number — this is where the earlier class-imbalance chart matters: a rare label like "animal" can look fine in an aggregate accuracy score while actually performing badly.

In [34]:
y_pred, y_true = learn.get_preds()

from sklearn.metrics import f1_score, classification_report

print("Macro F1:", f1_score(y_true, y_pred > 0.50, average='macro'))
print()
print(classification_report(y_true, y_pred > 0.50, target_names=photo_data.vocab, zero_division=1))

Concluding Reflections on Classification and Computer Vision¶

The lesson closes by stepping back from the code: any classification scheme — "illustrated vs. text-only," "human vs. animal vs. map" — is a simplification imposed on messier visual reality. A photo can be ambiguous, can show multiple things at once (hence multi-label), or can resist the categories entirely. The lesson draws on Borges' famous fictional taxonomy and Foucault's writing on classification to make the point that every classification scheme, computational or not, abstracts away nuance in order to be usable at scale.

Reflection question 6: Both of my computer vision tutorials involved a classification scheme that simplifies something messy: this one labels newspaper photos into fixed categories, and my facial recognition notebook labeled every face as either "happy" (smiling) or not. In your own words, what's one piece of real-world nuance that gets lost in each of those simplifications?
